subject: English

Period schedule:

Total: 4 periods · 3h 20min

periods.activity_title: Reading and Appreciating India's Patriotic Ode

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Reflect and Respond (p.23): odd-one-out vocabulary choices for four underlined poem words
Check Your Understanding (p.25): identify mood, tone, rhyme scheme, and personification
Reading for Appreciation (p.25): analyse impact of the recurring refrain

homework.task_brief: Check Your Understanding (p.25): fill-in-the-blank poem summary using ten box words

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the poem aloud with students following in their textbooks (p.23–24), attending to the refrain and the parallel structure created by hyphens in the first stanza. Students note any words or images that strike them on first hearing.

Students work individually on Reflect and Respond (p.23): the odd-one-out vocabulary task for four underlined words in the poem. Answers are shared aloud and the teacher draws attention to connotation differences among near-synonyms.

Whole-class guided reading of Check Your Understanding (p.25): students complete the features table — mood, tone, rhyme scheme, and examples of personification — with teacher prompting for evidence from the poem text.

Students respond in writing to the refrain-impact question from Reading for Appreciation (p.25), then two or three volunteers share their responses; teacher consolidates by noting the chant-like, unifying function of the refrain.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem's dominant device is apostrophe — India addressed as 'she' — which underpins every personification answer students will give; drawing this out early sharpens the rest of the appreciation work. Students often conflate mood and tone; use the reverential, celebratory mood versus the passionate patriotic tone as a concrete contrast. The fill-in-the-blank poem summary (p.25) is set as self-study; students who need a prompt may use the poem text.

periods.activity_title: Word-Building with Suffixes from the Poem

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Vocabulary in Context (p.29): complete suffix table using words found in the poem
Vocabulary in Context (p.30): add new suffixes to form words and write original sentences

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly recaps the poem's language, asking students to recall the most striking words from the text — 'peerless', 'auspicious', 'antiquity', 'divinest' — and writes them on the board. The class identifies which suffix each word carries.

Students complete the Vocabulary in Context suffix table (p.29): they scan the poem for words carrying the suffixes -ous, -ity, -est, and -less, record one example each, and note the meaning the suffix adds. Pairs compare answers before whole-class verification.

Students tackle the second Vocabulary in Context task (p.30): they select a base word, attach each of the four new suffixes (-tion, -ive, -ment, -ed), and compose one original sentence per formed word. The teacher circulates, prompting students to choose sentences thematically linked to India's landscape or heritage.

periods.teacher_notes: Both suffix tasks are grounded in the poem's actual lexis — 'auspicious' (-ous), 'antiquity' (-ity), 'divinest' (-est), 'peerless' (-less) — so the textbook scan is purposeful rather than arbitrary. A common pitfall is students writing the same base word for multiple suffixes; prompt them to try different roots for each slot. Encourage sentences that echo the poem's world (rivers, mountains, scripture) to keep vocabulary and content connected.

periods.activity_title: Listening to Travellers, Speaking About Home

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Listen and Respond (p.30): identify speakers from two pictures of travellers
Listen and Respond (p.31): match statements to speakers, discarding two distractors
Speaking Activity (p.31): paired praise of home village/town/city using provided cues

time_bands.activity: Teacher prepares the class for the listening activity by briefly orienting them: four speakers describe their favourite travel destinations in India, connecting to the poem's celebration of India's diverse landscapes.

Teacher reads the transcript aloud twice (Transcript p.260). First listening: students identify which speaker belongs to each of the two pictures — hiker and rock-climber (p.30). Second listening: students complete the matching task (p.31), pairing five of the six statements to the correct speaker and identifying the two distractors.
Quick whole-class check of listening answers; teacher probes reasoning — 'Which words told you that Speaker 2 was the rock-climber?' — to reinforce attention to detail and summarising skills.

Pairs take turns praising their home village, town, or city using the six cue prompts in the Speaking Activity (p.31). After each partner speaks, the listener responds briefly — agreeing, adding a point, or offering a different perspective with reasons. Two or three pairs share with the whole class.

periods.teacher_notes: The listening transcript (p.260 of the appendix) features four speakers describing nature destinations — riverbank, mountains, desert, forests — all of which the poem alludes to through its imagery of Himavant, Ganga, and the 'sunny golden land'; the teacher can use this echo to deepen engagement. A common pitfall in the matching task is that statements 1 and 4 (green surroundings and risk/thrill) sound similar to multiple speakers; guide students to listen for the specific occupation or emotion each speaker names. For the speaking task, students who struggle to begin may use the cue 'I feel a deep sense of pride when I think about…' as an entry point.

periods.activity_title: Writing a Travel Memory and Exploring Patriotic Texts

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Writing Task (p.31): guided paragraph about a memorable place visited
Learning Beyond the Text (p.31): share a patriotic poem or song in a regional language

homework.task_brief: Learning Beyond the Text (p.31): group project on India's six major geographical feature categories

time_bands.activity: Teacher models the writing task by briefly narrating one memorable place she or he has visited, using the five scaffold questions on p.31 as a spoken outline. Students jot a quick plan — five bullet answers — for their own chosen place before beginning to write.

Students write their paragraph independently using the five scaffold questions (p.31): reason for visiting, travel companions, preparation, accommodation, and activities. Teacher circulates, prompting those who stall to begin with 'Why did you go there?'

Peer-response: students exchange drafts with a partner, who reads and marks one strong descriptive detail and one place where more vivid language would help. Writers read the feedback and make a quick revision before handing in.

Beyond-the-Text sharing: three or four volunteers recite or quote a patriotic poem or song they know in their regional language (p.31), offer a brief explanation of its meaning in English or Hindi, and invite a classmate reaction. The teacher notes the thematic parallels with Subramania Bharati's celebration of India.

periods.teacher_notes: Having celebrated India's rivers, mountains, and spiritual heritage through the poem, students typically find a personal travel memory accessible as a writing anchor; the teacher may suggest that students whose place is unfamiliar to others pay special attention to descriptive detail. A common pitfall is a list-like paragraph that answers the five questions mechanically without cohesion; the modelled oral outline at the opening helps students see how the five points can flow. The interdisciplinary geography project (p.31) is assigned as self-study for groups to complete outside class.
materials: Students' own knowledge of regional-language poems or songs

items.source_lo: Student analyses poetic devices, tone, mood, and the effect of structural choices using a poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Patriotic ode to India celebrating Himavant, Ganga, Upanishads, warriors, and Buddha's dhamma.
items.item_stem:
Read the second stanza on p.24, beginning “Gallant warriors have lived here.” Choose the option that best describes the mood created by this stanza.

A. Sorrowful and elegiac, mourning heroes who are gone
B. Reverential and celebratory, honouring India’s human and cultural legacy
C. Anxious and uncertain, questioning whether the greatness will last
D. Detached and factual, listing historical achievements without emotion

options.label: A
options.text: Sorrowful and elegiac, mourning heroes who are gone

options.label: B
options.text: Reverential and celebratory, honouring India’s human and cultural legacy

options.label: C
options.text: Anxious and uncertain, questioning whether the greatness will last

options.label: D
options.text: Detached and factual, listing historical achievements without emotion

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student has confused the celebratory tone with elegy; the stanza honours, it does not mourn.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student has imposed uncertainty onto the poem; the stanza makes confident assertions of India’s greatness.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student has missed the emotive language — ‘gallant’, ‘sanctified’, ‘divinest’ — that elevates the stanza beyond a factual list.

items.source_lo: Student analyses poetic devices, tone, mood, and the effect of structural choices using a poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Patriotic ode to India celebrating Himavant, Ganga, Upanishads, warriors, and Buddha's dhamma.
items.item_stem:
Read the first stanza on p.23, beginning “The mighty Himavant is ours.”

1. Identify the structural device used in this stanza and explain how it shapes the reader’s experience of the poem.
2. The refrain ‘she’s peerless, let’s praise her!’ recurs at the close of each stanza. Evaluate how this refrain contributes to both the tone and the overall effect of the poem as an ode.
items.visual_stimulus: Read the first stanza on p.23, beginning “The mighty Himavant is ours.”

expected_elements: Identifies the parallel structure: each line pairs a treasure with a rhetorical assertion.
Explains that hyphens create deliberate pauses, reinforcing admiration and chant-like rhythm.
Notes the refrain unifies the three stanzas into a single sustained act of praise.
Links the refrain to tone: passionate patriotism, elevated and reverential.
Connects refrain and apostrophe: addressing India as ‘she’ personalises the ode.

items.source_context: Four speakers describe favourite Indian travel destinations — riverbank, mountains, desert, forests.
items.item_stem:
Listen to the four speakers. For each statement below, write True or False.

1. Speaker 1 describes the Narmada riverbank as a place for reflection and inner harmony.
2. Speaker 2 says that visiting the Western Ghats made adventure sports feel boring.
3. Speaker 3 is a photographer who finds desert landscapes matchless at sunset.
4. Speaker 4 is a travel vlogger whose recent trip was to the Andaman Islands.

options.text: Speaker 1 describes the Narmada riverbank as a place for reflection and inner harmony.
Speaker 2 says that visiting the Western Ghats made adventure sports feel boring.
Speaker 3 is a photographer who finds desert landscapes matchless at sunset.
Speaker 4 is a travel vlogger whose recent trip was to the Andaman Islands.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1 — True: Speaker 1 explicitly says the Narmada riverside helped him reflect, meditate, and find inner harmony. 2 — False: Speaker 2 says the Western Ghats changed everything for him and the mountains are his playground; he never calls adventure sports boring. 3 — True: Speaker 3 identifies as a photographer and calls the desert’s sunset colours matchless. 4 — False: Speaker 4 visited the Sundarbans, not the Andaman Islands.

items.source_lo: Student identifies speaker and matches descriptive details to sources by listening attentively to spoken accounts.
items.source_context: Four speakers describe favourite Indian travel destinations — riverbank, mountains, desert, forests.
items.item_stem: After listening to the four speakers again, answer in 2–3 sentences: Speaker 1 and Speaker 4 both describe experiences in nature, yet they value very different qualities in their destinations. What does each speaker value, and what does the contrast reveal about the diversity of India’s natural landscapes?

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Speaker 1 values the serene quietness of the Narmada riverbank for reflection, meditation, and inner harmony, while Speaker 4 values the biodiversity of the Sundarbans forest as a vlogger who wants to share nature’s wonders. The contrast shows that India’s natural landscapes range from calm, contemplative riverside settings to rich, dynamic forest ecosystems, each offering a distinct human experience.

items.item_stem: Describe a geographical or cultural feature of your village, town, or city that you find remarkable. Speak for about a minute, mentioning what the feature is, why it matters to the community, and what a visitor should know about it.

expected_elements: Names a specific geographical or cultural feature of their place.
Explains why the feature matters to the local community.
Includes at least one detail a visitor would find useful or striking.
Uses appropriate vocabulary of praise and admiration.

items.source_lo: Student articulates praise and admiration for a familiar place, supporting claims with reasons in paired oral exchange.
items.source_context: Paired spoken praise of a student’s own village, town, or city using provided expression cues.
items.item_stem: Your partner has just praised a feature of their village or town. Do you agree that local places deserve as much celebration as national landmarks like the Himalayas or the Ganga? State your position clearly and support it with at least two reasons.

expected_elements: States a clear position — agreement, partial agreement, or disagreement.
Offers at least two reasons that support the stated position.
Engages with the partner’s point rather than ignoring it.
Uses language of reasoned argument, not just assertion.

items.item_stem: Write a paragraph (80–100 words) describing a visit to a historically significant place in India. Include: why you went there, who accompanied you, and one detail about the place that stayed with you.

expected_elements: Names a specific historically significant place in India.
States the reason for the visit and who came along.
Includes one concrete, vivid detail that makes the place memorable.
Organises ideas in a logical sequence with a clear opening and closing.

items.item_stem: Write a letter to the editor of your school magazine (120–150 words) arguing that Indian students should be encouraged to visit heritage sites in their own state before travelling abroad. Support your argument with at least two specific reasons, and conclude with a clear recommendation.

expected_elements: Uses formal letter-to-editor format: date, salutation, sign-off.
States the argument clearly in the opening paragraph.
Provides at least two specific, reasoned arguments for the claim.
Concludes with a concrete recommendation addressed to readers or authorities.
Maintains a formal, persuasive register throughout.

items.item_stem: Add the suffix -ment to the word ‘enrich’ (enrichment) and add the suffix -ive to the word ‘express’ (expressive). Write one sentence each using the two newly formed words. Each sentence must relate to India’s cultural or natural heritage as described in the poem.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Acceptable responses form ‘enrichment’ and ‘expressive’ correctly and use each in a sentence that references India’s heritage, landscape, or spiritual tradition — for example: ‘The enrichment of Indian civilisation owes much to the teachings of the Buddha.’ and ‘The poet’s language is expressive of deep admiration for the Ganga’s grace.’

items.item_stem: Name a patriotic poem or folk song you know in a regional language. Write 3–4 sentences explaining: what the poem or song celebrates, what language it is in, and how its theme connects to the idea of pride in India’s heritage.

expected_elements: Names a specific regional-language poem or song by title or first line.
Identifies the language and briefly describes what the text celebrates.
Makes an explicit thematic connection to Indian heritage or natural beauty.
Uses own words; avoids vague generalisations about ‘India being great.’

items.item_stem: Design a project plan (in note form) for an interdisciplinary study of one of India’s major geographical regions — mountains, river valleys, or forests. Your plan must name: (a) the specific region, (b) one language spoken there, (c) one cultural or historical fact about the region, and (d) a creative output your group would produce to share the findings.

expected_elements: Names a specific Indian geographical region (e.g. Himalayan foothills, Gangetic plain).
Correctly identifies a language spoken in that region.
States one cultural or historical fact grounded in real knowledge.
Proposes a creative output — poster, bilingual poem, video script, or map.
Plan is coherent and shows interdisciplinary thinking linking geography and culture.
